verses.zh: 耶稣又对门徒说：「有一个财主的管家，别人向他主人告他浪费主人的财物。
verses.en: Jesus[NOTE:1] also said to the disciples, “There was a rich man who was informed of accusations[NOTE:2] that his manager[NOTE:3] was wasting[NOTE:4] his assets.
notes: Grk “He”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
These are not formal legal charges, but reports from friends, acquaintances, etc.; Grk “A certain man was rich who had a manager, and this one was reported to him as wasting his property.”
His manager was the steward in charge of managing the house. He could have been a slave trained for the role.
Or “squandering.” This verb is graphic; it means to scatter (L&N 57.151).

verses.zh: 主人叫他来，对他说：『我听见你这事怎么样呢？把你所经管的交代明白，因你不能再作我的管家。』
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] he called the manager[NOTE:2] in and said to him, ‘What is this I hear about you?[NOTE:3] Turn in the account of your administration,[NOTE:4] because you can no longer be my manager.’
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “so” to indicate the result of the reports the man received about his manager.
Grk “him”; the referent (the manager) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Although phrased as a question, the charges were believed by the owner, as his dismissal of the manager implies.
Or “stewardship”; the Greek word οἰκονομία (oikonomia) is cognate with the noun for the manager (οἰκονόμος, oikonomos).

verses.zh: 那管家心里说：『主人辞我，不用我再作管家，我将来做甚么？锄地呢？无力；讨饭呢？怕羞。
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] the manager said to himself, ‘What should I do, since my master is taking my position[NOTE:2] away from me? I’m not strong enough to dig,[NOTE:3] and I’m too ashamed[NOTE:4] to beg.
notes: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events in the parable.
Grk “the stewardship,” “the management.”

Here “dig” could refer (1) to excavation (“dig ditches,” L&N 19.55) or (2) to agricultural labor (“work the soil,” L&N 43.3). In either case this was labor performed by the uneducated, so it would be an insult as a job for a manager.

To beg would represent a real lowering of status for the manager, because many of those whom he had formerly collected debts from, he would now be forced to beg from.tn Grk “I do not have strength to dig; I am ashamed to beg.”

verses.zh: 我知道怎么行，好叫人在我不作管家之后，接我到他们家里去。』
verses.en: I know[NOTE:1] what to do so that when I am put out of management, people will welcome me into their homes.’[NOTE:2]
notes: This is a dramatic use of the aorist and the verse is left unconnected to the previous verse by asyndeton, giving the impression of a sudden realization.
Thinking ahead, the manager develops a plan to make people think kindly of him (welcome me into their homes).

verses.zh: 于是把欠他主人债的，一个一个地叫了来，问头一个说：『你欠我主人多少？』
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] he contacted[NOTE:2] his master’s debtors one by one. He asked the first, ‘How much do you owe my master?’
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “so” to indicate the result of the manager’s decision.
Grk “summoning.” The participle προσκαλεσάμενος (proskalesamenos) has been translated as a finite verb due to requirements of contemporary English style.

verses.zh: 他说：『一百篓（每篓约五十斤）油。』管家说：『拿你的帐，快坐下，写五十。』
verses.en: The man[NOTE:1] replied, ‘100 measures[NOTE:2] of olive oil.’ The manager[NOTE:3] said to him, ‘Take your bill, sit down quickly, and write 50.’[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “He”; the referent (the first debtor) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

A measure (sometimes translated “bath”) was just over 8 gallons (about 30 liters). This is a large debt—about 875 gallons (3000 liters) of olive oil, worth 1000 denarii, over three year’s pay for a daily worker.
Grk “He”; the referent (the manager) has been specified in the translation for clarity. Here δέ (de) has not been translated for stylistic reasons.

The bill was halved (sit down quickly, and write 50). What was the steward doing? This is debated. 1) Did he simply lower the price? 2) Did he remove interest from the debt? 3) Did he remove his own commission? It is hard to be sure. Either of the latter two options is more likely. The goal was clear: The manager would be seen in a favorable light for bringing a deflationary trend to prices.

verses.zh: 又问一个说：『你欠多少？』他说：『一百石麦子。』管家说：『拿你的帐，写八十。』
verses.en: Then he said to another, ‘And how much do you owe?’ The second man[NOTE:1] replied, ‘100 measures[NOTE:2] of wheat.’ The manager[NOTE:3] said to him, ‘Take your bill, and write 80.’[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “He”; the referent (the second debtor) has been specified in the translation for clarity. Here δέ (de) has not been translated for stylistic reasons.

The 100 measures here was 100 cors. A cor was a Hebrew dry measure for grain, flour, etc., of between 10-12 bushels (about 390 liters). This was a huge amount of wheat, representing the yield of about 100 acres, a debt of between 2500-3000 denarii.
Grk “He”; the referent (the manager) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
The percentage of reduction may not be as great because of the change in material.

verses.zh: 主人就夸奖这不义的管家做事聪明；因为今世之子，在世事之上，较比光明之子更加聪明。
verses.en: The[NOTE:1] master commended the dishonest[NOTE:2] manager because he acted shrewdly.[NOTE:3] For the people[NOTE:4] of this world are more shrewd in dealing with their contemporaries[NOTE:5] than the people[NOTE:6] of light.
notes: Grk “And the.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.

Is the manager dishonest because of what he just did? Or is it a reference to what he had done earlier, described in v. 1? This is a difficult question, but it seems unlikely that the master, having fired the man for prior dishonesty, would now commend those same actions. It would also be unusual for Jesus to make that point of the story the example. Thus it is more likely the reference to dishonesty goes back to the earliest events, while the commendation is for the cleverness of the former manager reflected in vv. 5-7.

Where this parable ends is debated: Does it conclude with v. 7, after v. 8a, after v. 8b, or after v. 9? Verse 8a looks as if it is still part of the story, with its clear reference to the manager, while 8b looks like Jesus’ application, since its remarks are more general. So it is most likely the parable stops after v. 8a.
Grk “sons” (an idiom).
Grk “with their own generation.”
Grk “sons.” Here the phrase “sons of light” is a reference to the righteous. The point is that those of the world often think ahead about consequences better than the righteous do.

verses.zh: 我又告诉你们，要藉着那不义的钱财结交朋友，到了钱财无用的时候，他们可以接你们到永存的帐幕里去。
verses.en: And I tell you, make friends for yourselves by how you use worldly wealth,[NOTE:1] so that when it runs out, you will be welcomed[NOTE:2] into the eternal homes.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “unrighteous mammon.” Mammon is the Aramaic term for wealth or possessions. The point is not that money is inherently evil, but that it is often misused so that it is a means of evil; see 1 Tim 6:6-10, 17-19. The call is to be generous and kind in its use. Zacchaeus becomes the example of this in Luke’s Gospel (19:1-10).
Grk “they may welcome you.”
Grk “eternal tents” (as dwelling places).

verses.zh: 人在最小的事上忠心，在大事上也忠心；在最小的事上不义，在大事上也不义。
verses.en: “The one who is faithful in a very little[NOTE:1] is also faithful in much, and the one who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.
notes: The point of the statement faithful in a very little is that character is shown in how little things are treated.

verses.zh: 倘若你们在不义的钱财上不忠心，谁还把那真实的钱财托付你们呢？
verses.en: If then you haven’t been trustworthy[NOTE:1] in handling worldly wealth,[NOTE:2] who will entrust you with the true riches?[NOTE:3]
notes: Or “faithful.”
Grk “the unrighteous mammon.” See the note on the phrase “worldly wealth” in v. 9.
Entrust you with the true riches is a reference to future service for God. The idea is like 1 Cor 9:11, except there the imagery is reversed.

verses.zh: 倘若你们在别人的东西上不忠心，谁还把你们自己的东西给你们呢？
verses.en: And if you haven’t been trustworthy[NOTE:1] with someone else’s property,[NOTE:2] who will give you your own[NOTE:3]?
notes: Or “faithful.”
Grk “have not been faithful with what is another’s.”
Grk “what is your own.”

verses.zh: 一个仆人不能事奉两个主；不是恶这个爱那个，就是重这个轻那个。你们不能又事奉　神，又事奉玛门。」
verses.en: No servant can serve two masters, for either he will hate[NOTE:1] the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise[NOTE:2] the other. You cannot serve God and money.”[NOTE:3]
notes: The contrast between hate and love here is rhetorical. The point is that one will choose the favorite if a choice has to be made.
Or “and treat [the other] with contempt.”

The term money is used to translate mammon, the Aramaic term for wealth or possessions. The point is not that money is inherently evil, but that it is often misused so that it is a means of evil; see 1 Tim 6:6-10, 17-19. Here “money” is personified as a potential master and thus competes with God for the loyalty of the disciple. The passage is ultimately not a condemnation of wealth (there is no call here for absolute poverty) but a call for unqualified discipleship. God must be first, not money or possessions.tn Grk “God and mammon.” This is the same word (μαμωνᾶς, mamōnas; often merely transliterated as “mammon”) translated “worldly wealth” in vv. 9, 11.

verses.zh: 法利赛人是贪爱钱财的；他们听见这一切话，就嗤笑耶稣。
verses.en: The Pharisees[NOTE:1] (who loved money) heard all this and ridiculed[NOTE:2] him.
notes: See the note on Pharisees in 5:17.
A figurative extension of the literal meaning “to turn one’s nose up at someone”; here “ridicule, sneer at, show contempt for” (L&N 33.409).

verses.zh: 耶稣对他们说：「你们是在人面前自称为义的，你们的心，　神却知道；因为人所尊贵的，是　神看为可憎恶的。
verses.en: But[NOTE:1] Jesus[NOTE:2] said to them, “You are the ones who justify yourselves in men’s eyes,[NOTE:3] but God knows your hearts. For what is highly prized[NOTE:4] among men is utterly detestable[NOTE:5] in God’s sight.
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “but” to indicate the contrast present in this context.
Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

Grk “before men.” The contrast is between outward appearance (“in people’s eyes”) and inward reality (“God knows your hearts”). Here the Greek term ἄνθρωπος (anthrōpos) is used twice in a generic sense, referring to both men and women, but “men” has been retained in the text to provide a strong verbal contrast with “God” in the second half of the verse.
Or “exalted.” This refers to the pride that often comes with money and position.
Or “is an abomination,” “is abhorrent” (L&N 25.187).

verses.zh: 律法和先知到约翰为止，从此　神国的福音传开了，人人努力要进去。
verses.en: “The law and the prophets were in force[NOTE:1] until John;[NOTE:2] since then,[NOTE:3] the good news of the kingdom of God[NOTE:4] has been proclaimed, and everyone is urged to enter it.[NOTE:5]
notes: There is no verb in the Greek text; one must be supplied. Some translations (NASB, NIV) supply “proclaimed” based on the parallelism with the proclamation of the kingdom. The transitional nature of this verse, however, seems to call for something more like “in effect” (NRSV) or, as used here, “in force.” Further, Greek generally can omit one of two kinds of verbs—either the equative verb or one that is already mentioned in the preceding context (ExSyn 39).
John refers to John the Baptist.
Until John; since then. This verse indicates a shift in era, from law to kingdom.

The kingdom of God is a major theme of Jesus’ teaching. The nature of the kingdom of God in the NT and in Jesus’ teaching has long been debated by interpreters and scholars, with discussion primarily centering around the nature of the kingdom (earthly, heavenly, or both) and the kingdom’s arrival (present, future, or both). An additional major issue concerns the relationship between the kingdom of God and the person and work of Jesus himself. See Luke 6:20; 11:20; 17:20-21.

Many translations have “entereth violently into it” (ASV) or “is forcing his way into it” (NASB, NIV “forcing their way into it”). This is not true of everyone. It is better to read the verb βιάζεται here as passive rather than middle, and in a softened sense of “be urged.” See Gen 33:11; Judg 13:15-16; 19:7; 2 Sam 3:25, 27 in the LXX. This fits the context well because it agrees with Jesus’ attempt to persuade his opponents to respond morally. For further discussion and details, see D. L. Bock, Luke (BECNT), 2:1352-53. For a summary of the lexical options see BDAG 175 s.v. βιάζω. Differences in the context suggest a different meaning for the same term in Matt 11:12.

verses.zh: 天地废去较比律法的一点一画落空还容易。
verses.en: But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one tiny stroke of a letter[NOTE:1] in the law to become void.[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “one small part of a letter” (L&N 33.37).
Grk “to fall”; that is, “to drop out of the text.” Jesus’ point may be that the law is going to reach its goal without fail, in that the era of the promised kingdom comes.

verses.zh: 凡休妻另娶的就是犯奸淫；娶被休之妻的也是犯奸淫。」
verses.en: “Everyone who divorces his wife and marries[NOTE:1] someone else commits adultery, and the one who marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery.
notes: The examples of marriage and divorce show that the ethical standards of the new era are still faithful to promises made in the presence of God. To contribute to the breakup of a marriage, which involved a vow before God, is to commit adultery. This works whether one gets a divorce or marries a person who is divorced, thus finalizing the breakup of the marriage. Jesus’ point concerns the need for fidelity and ethical integrity in the new era.

verses.zh: 「有一个财主穿着紫色袍和细麻布衣服，天天奢华宴乐。
verses.en: “There was a rich man who dressed in purple[NOTE:1] and fine linen and who feasted sumptuously[NOTE:2] every day.
notes: Purple describes a fine, expensive dye used on luxurious clothing, and by metonymy, refers to clothing colored with that dye. It pictures someone of great wealth.
Or “celebrated with ostentation” (L&N 88.255), that is, with showing off. Here was the original conspicuous consumer.

verses.zh: 又有一个讨饭的，名叫拉撒路，浑身生疮，被人放在财主门口，
verses.en: But at his gate lay[NOTE:1] a poor man named Lazarus[NOTE:2] whose body was covered with sores,[NOTE:3]
notes: The passive verb ἐβέβλητο (ebeblēto) does not indicate how Lazarus got there. Cf. BDAG 163 s.v. βάλλω 1.b, “he lay before the door”; Josephus, Ant. 9.10.2 (9.209).
This is the one time in all the gospels that a figure in a parable is mentioned by name. It will become important later in the account.
Or “was covered with ulcers.” The words “whose body” are implied in the context (L&N 23.180).

verses.zh: 要得财主桌子上掉下来的零碎充饥；并且狗来舔他的疮。
verses.en: who longed to eat[NOTE:1] what fell from the rich man’s table. In addition, the dogs[NOTE:2] came and licked[NOTE:3] his sores.
notes: Grk “to eat his fill,” but this phrase has been simplified as “to eat” for stylistic reasons.
The term κύνες (kunes) refers to “wild” dogs (either “street” dogs or watchdogs), not house pets (L&N 4.34).
When the dogs came and licked his sores it meant that he was unclean. See the negative image of Rev 22:15 that draws on this picture.

verses.zh: 后来那讨饭的死了，被天使带去放在亚伯拉罕的怀里。财主也死了，并且埋葬了。
verses.en: “Now[NOTE:1] the poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham’s side.[NOTE:2] The[NOTE:3] rich man also died and was buried.[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “Now it happened that the.” The introductory phrase ἐγένετο (egeneto, “it happened that”), common in Luke (69 times) and Acts (54 times), is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated.
Grk “to Abraham’s bosom.” The phrase “carried by the angels to Abraham’s bosom” describes being gathered to the fathers and is a way to refer to heaven (Gen 15:15; 47:30; Deut 31:16).
Grk “And the.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
The shorter description suggests a different fate, which is confirmed in the following verses.

verses.zh: 他在阴间受痛苦，举目远远地望见亚伯拉罕，又望见拉撒路在他怀里，
verses.en: And in Hades,[NOTE:1] as he was in torment,[NOTE:2] he looked up[NOTE:3] and saw Abraham far off with Lazarus at his side.[NOTE:4]
notes: The Greek term Hades stands for the Hebrew concept of Sheol. This is where the dead were gathered (Pss 16:10; 86:13). In the NT Hades sometimes has an additional negative force of awaiting judgment (Rev 20:13).
Hades is a place of torment, especially as one knows that he is separated from God.
Grk “he lifted up his eyes” (an idiom).
Grk “in his bosom,” the same phrase used in 16:22. This idiom refers to heaven and/or participation in the eschatological banquet. An appropriate modern equivalent is “at Abraham’s side.”

verses.zh: 就喊着说：『我祖亚伯拉罕哪，可怜我吧！打发拉撒路来，用指头尖蘸点水，凉凉我的舌头；因为我在这火焰里，极其痛苦。』
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] he called out,[NOTE:2] ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus[NOTE:3] to dip the tip of his finger[NOTE:4] in water and cool my tongue because I am in anguish[NOTE:5] in this fire.’[NOTE:6]
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “so” to indicate the implied result of previous actions in the narrative.
Grk “calling out he said”; this is redundant in contemporary English style and has been simplified to “he called out.”

The rich man had not helped Lazarus before, when he lay outside his gate (v. 20), but he knew him well enough to know his name. This is why the use of the name Lazarus in the parable is significant. (The rich man’s name, on the other hand, is not mentioned because it is not significant for the point of the story.)

The dipping of the tip of his finger in water is evocative of thirst. The thirsty are in need of God’s presence (Ps 42:1-2; Isa 5:13). The imagery suggests the rich man is now separated from the presence of God.
Or “in terrible pain” (L&N 24.92).
Fire in this context is OT imagery; see Isa 66:24.

verses.zh: 亚伯拉罕说：『儿啊，你该回想你生前享过福，拉撒路也受过苦；如今他在这里得安慰，你倒受痛苦。
verses.en: But Abraham said, ‘Child,[NOTE:1] remember that in your lifetime you received your good things and Lazarus likewise bad things, but now he is comforted here and you are in anguish.[NOTE:2]
notes: The Greek term here is τέκνον (teknon), which could be understood as a term of endearment.
Or “in terrible pain” (L&N 24.92). Here is the reversal Jesus mentioned in Luke 6:20-26.

verses.zh: 不但这样，并且在你我之间，有深渊限定，以致人要从这边过到你们那边是不能的；要从那边过到我们这边也是不能的。』
verses.en: Besides all this,[NOTE:1] a great chasm[NOTE:2] has been fixed between us,[NOTE:3] so that those who want to cross over from here to you cannot do so, and no one can cross from there to us.’
notes: Grk “And in all these things.” There is no way Lazarus could carry out this request even if divine justice were not involved.
The great chasm between heaven and hell is impassable forever. The rich man’s former status meant nothing now.
Grk “between us and you.”

verses.zh: 财主说：『我祖啊！既是这样，求你打发拉撒路到我父家去；
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] the rich man[NOTE:2] said, ‘Then I beg you, father—send Lazarus[NOTE:3] to my father’s house
notes: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “so” to indicate the rich man’s response to Abraham’s words.
Grk “he”; the referent (the rich man, v. 19) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Grk “Then I beg you, father, that you send him”; the referent (Lazarus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 因为我还有五个弟兄，他可以对他们作见证，免得他们也来到这痛苦的地方。』
verses.en: (for I have five brothers) to warn[NOTE:1] them so that they don’t come[NOTE:2] into this place of torment.’
notes: To warn them. The warning would consist of a call to act differently than their dead brother had, or else meet his current terrible fate.
Grk “lest they also come.”

verses.zh: 亚伯拉罕说：『他们有摩西和先知的话可以听从。』
verses.en: But Abraham said,[NOTE:1] ‘They have Moses and the prophets; they must respond to[NOTE:2] them.’
notes: Grk “says.” This is one of the few times Luke uses the historical present.
Or “obey”; Grk “hear.” This recalls the many OT texts calling for a righteous heart to respond to people in need (Deut 14:28-29; Isa 3:14-15; Amos 2:6-8; Mic 2:1-2; Zech 7:9-10).

verses.zh: 他说：『我祖亚伯拉罕哪，不是的，若有一个从死里复活的，到他们那里去的，他们必要悔改。』
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] the rich man[NOTE:2] said, ‘No, father Abraham, but if someone from the dead[NOTE:3] goes to them, they will repent.’
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
Grk “he”; the referent (the rich man, v. 19) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

If someone from the dead goes to them. The irony and joy of the story is that what is denied the rich man’s brothers, a word of warning from beyond the grave, is given to the reader of the Gospel in this exchange.

verses.zh: 亚伯拉罕说：『若不听从摩西和先知的话，就是有一个从死里复活的，他们也是不听劝。』」
verses.en: He[NOTE:1] replied to him, ‘If they do not respond to[NOTE:2] Moses and the prophets, they will not be convinced even if someone rises from the dead.’”[NOTE:3]
notes: Here δέ (de) has not been translated.
Or “obey”; Grk “hear.” See the note on the phrase “respond to” in v. 29.

The concluding statement of the parable, they will not be convinced even if someone rises from the dead, provides a hint that even Jesus’ resurrection will not help some to respond. The message of God should be good enough. Scripture is the sign to be heeded.
